title: The Silk Road
hookLine: monks traveled with merchants along the caravan roads into Central Asia and China

cards: Dust, bells and the slow sway of camels. A caravan winds between desert and mountain, loaded with cloth, spices and silver. Near the back, in robes the color of the dust, walk a few monks.
They carry almost nothing: a bowl, a few manuscripts, a teaching memorized by heart. The merchants are glad of them. Monks bless the journey, and some merchants give food and shelter in return.
At the oasis towns along the way, small monasteries begin to appear. The northern road is open: the Silk Road.

teach.h: A WEB OF ROADS, NOT ONE ROAD.
teach.b: First, the name. Silk Road is a modern label for a web of caravan routes, not one road, running from the edges of India and Persia, through Central Asia, into China. Goods moved along it, and so did ideas.
Second, traders were in the story from the start.

The Vinaya, the monks' rulebook, tells of two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, traveling with a caravan, who met the Buddha soon after his awakening, offered him food, and took refuge in him and his teaching.

Places like Khotan and Kucha, ringed by desert, grew rich on trade, and Buddhist monasteries rose there with merchant money. Monks learned the local languages, and the oases became schools and way stations.

The caves carved and painted along these routes still show donors in their best clothes, kneeling beside the Buddha. Fourth, why it worked. A merchant needs trust, a safe night, and a blessing for the road.
A monk needs food, company, and a way across the desert.

teach.h: EACH GAVE WHAT THE OTHER LACKED.
teach.b: Each gave the other what they lacked.
So, as historians tell it, the teaching didn't arrive in China by army. Much of it walked in, one caravan at a time, beside the people carrying silk the other way.

how: Buddhist monks have long depended on lay supporters for food and shelter, and merchants and business owners are often among the donors who support monasteries.

games.q: you're a merchant leading a caravan, and two monks ask to travel with you. what do you do?
o: turn them away: they carry nothing to trade.
take them along, and give them food.
charge them the same as any trader.
games.why: merchants were often glad of monks: they blessed the journey, and merchants gave food, shelter and money for monasteries.

practice: Let the breath slow to the pace of walking animals, and picture the line of camels, the bells, the dust, and the monks near the back.
Walk beside them: each in-breath a step, each out-breath a step, nowhere to hurry, the oasis still far off. If your mind wanders off the road, come back to the next step.

wordCard.voice: Bhikkhu. A monk, like the ones who walked near the back of the caravans along the Silk Road, carrying almost nothing.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bhikṣu (Pali bhikkhu), a monk, like the ones walking with the caravans.
